title: Plant for later
hook: Honi's carob tree again: what will grow after you? (Talmud, Taanit 23a)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a life pressed into a line on a stone. Your line was six words. Did yours come, and did you write it down? Day eight hundred six.

A man is walking along a road and sees someone on his knees in the dirt, planting a carob tree. The walker stops and asks how long it will take before the tree bears fruit. Seventy years, says the planter. The walker asks the obvious next question: are you so sure you'll live another seventy years? The walker is Honi, a sage the Talmud remembers in the tractate Taanit, and this may not be the first time you've met him on this path. Today the story comes back, at the end of a block about grief, with a new question: what will grow after you?
screen: `A MAN PLANTING A CAROB TREE.` → `"SEVENTY YEARS."` → `WHAT GROWS AFTER YOU?`

segments.voice: First, the planter's answer. In the Talmud's telling, he says, more or less: I found the world with carob trees in it. As my ancestors planted for me, so I plant for my children. He isn't planting for himself. He's paying forward a gift he never saw being given. Second, Honi sleeps. Honi sits down to eat, sleep comes over him, and a rock formation closes around him so that no one sees him. He sleeps for seventy years. When he wakes, he sees a man gathering carobs from that same tree, and asks: are you the one who planted it? The man answers: I'm his grandson. Third, an ending that isn't sweet. The Talmud doesn't stop there. Honi goes home and to the house of study, and nobody believes he is who he says. No one gives him the honor he was used to. In his loneliness he asks for death, and he dies. Some readers hear the two halves of the story together: a tree can outlive its planter, and a person still needs companions while they're alive. Fourth, what the dead leave planted. In a week of grief, the story turns the question around. The people we've lost planted things we still eat from: a recipe, a way of giving thanks at the table, a habit of showing up, a garden, a joke the family still tells. And the living can plant too, things whose fruit they won't be around to taste. The instruction is short: plant for later.
screen: `AS MY ANCESTORS PLANTED FOR ME` · `HONI SLEEPS, THE TREE GROWS` · `AN ENDING THAT ISN'T SWEET` · `WHAT THE DEAD LEFT PLANTED` · then, large: `PLANT FOR LATER.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one thing someone before you planted that you still live from: a recipe, a saying, a habit, a skill they taught you, an actual tree. Give them a moment of thanks, in whatever way is yours. Then choose one small thing you could begin that will outlast this week, maybe this life: a seed in a pot, a letter to a child to open later, teaching someone a skill, a kindness made into a habit. Hold that one thing in mind. The bell holds the time.
Plant for later: doing something now whose fruit you may never taste, as others once did for you. Today's word.
Your line: plant for later. Today, begin the one thing you chose, even if the first step is small enough to fit in a pocket. Day eight hundred six.

howItsDone: Some people answer a death by planting: a memorial tree, a scholarship, a garden bed, or simply passing on a recipe or skill the person taught them, so that something keeps growing after the loss.

notes: Taanit 23a paraphrased throughout (Rodkinson not quoted). 'Seventy years' appears in the text itself for both the tree and Honi's sleep.

Ending: Honi goes to his house and the study hall, is not believed or honored, asks for mercy/death, and dies; the Talmud then quotes 'either companionship or death'. The script paraphrases without quoting; check.
'This may not be the first time you've met him on this path' refers to an earlier Honi day (index says 'again'); writer did not confirm which day.
'a way of giving thanks at the table' is meant inclusively; trim if it reads oddly.
Editor: changed 'That's the whole instruction' so it doesn't echo day 797's 'That's the whole lesson in three words'.

Audit (2026-10-01): 'a way of saying grace or not' read as garbled; now 'a way of giving thanks at the table'. Honi appears earlier on this path (y1 days 57, 58, 63; y2 days 344, 428, 655), so the hook's 'may not be the first time' is accurate.
